analysis.one_liner: Requires the government to negotiate Medicare prescription drug prices with manufacturers.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on January 25, 2011 and never received a committee vote or any floor action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have directed the Secretary of Health and Human Services to negotiate the prices, including discounts and rebates, that drug manufacturers may charge Medicare's private prescription drug plans for covered Part D drugs. It would have struck the existing 'noninterference' rule, which bars the government from intervening in those negotiations, and required the Secretary to report to Congress every six months on the prices achieved. It explicitly did not allow the Secretary to impose a specific formulary or block plans from negotiating even deeper discounts.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly tens of millions of seniors and disabled people enrolled in Medicare Part D, whose out-of-pocket costs and premiums track the prices plans pay for drugs. The Medicare program itself would also benefit if plan bids — which set the government's premium subsidies — came in lower. Taxpayers fund most of Part D's cost, so lower negotiated prices would reduce federal spending.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Medicare Part D enrollees and taxpayers

how_it_helps.text: Amends Medicare Part D to direct the Secretary of Health and Human Services to negotiate with pharmaceutical manufacturers the prices, discounts, rebates, and other price concessions charged to prescription drug plan sponsors and Medicare Advantage organizations for covered Part D drugs.
Removes the existing statutory 'noninterference' provision that currently prohibits the Secretary from intervening in Part D drug price negotiations, replacing it with a negotiation mandate.

Requires the Secretary to report to the relevant House and Senate committees every six months on the negotiations conducted and the price discounts achieved for Medicare beneficiaries, starting by June 1, 2012.
Applies to plan years beginning January 1, 2012, so the savings could have started flowing to enrollees and the program quickly after enactment.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers would bear the cost in the form of lower prices and larger discounts on the single largest group drug purchase in the country. Private Medicare drug plans and their pharmacy intermediaries could see their negotiating role constrained, though the bill preserves their ability to seek discounts below the negotiated price.

drawbacks.text: The bill gives the Secretary no power to set a price, mandate a formulary, or walk away from a deal — only to negotiate — so the savings actually achieved could have been modest. Congressional budget analysts have historically estimated that Medicare negotiation without broader authority yields only small savings, since the government still pays market prices set largely by the manufacturers' patent position.

Allowing the largest buyer in the drug market to negotiate on behalf of everyone could concentrate pricing power in government hands, which manufacturers argue would reduce revenues available for research and development on future medicines. Supporters counter that other government programs, like the VA, already negotiate and pay far less for the same drugs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For Medicare beneficiaries and taxpayers, the upside is straightforward: lower prices on a benefit that taxpayers subsidize heavily and seniors pay for out of pocket. The honest caveat is design — because the bill leaves formularies and the underlying patent rules untouched, it buys bargaining power without real leverage, so the savings could fall well short of what direct price-setting would produce. Even so, it would have been a genuine step toward what every other large drug buyer, including the VA, already does.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up, so it died when the 112th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Amy Klobuchar introduced the bill on January 25, 2011, with Sen. Mark Begich, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance the same day.
Eight senators cosponsored the bill — seven Democrats and one Independent; no Republican signed on.
The action history shows no further action: no hearing, no committee vote, no floor consideration at any point during the 112th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers are better off because the bill died. Under current law the government is barred from negotiating Part D drug prices, and the largest single purchaser of prescription drugs in the country continues to pay prices set by the manufacturers; Medicare beneficiaries and taxpayers did not get the savings this bill would have pursued.

for.name: Sen. Amy Klobuchar
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on January 25, 2011 to require HHS to negotiate Medicare Part D drug prices.

for.name: Sen. Mark Begich
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor when the bill was introduced.

for.name: 7 Senate Democrats and 1 Independent senator
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it nine total supporters in the Senate.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Committee of referral under Chairman Max Baucus
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on January 25, 2011 and never held a markup or vote on the bill; it received no further action for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Pharmaceutical manufacturers and their trade association
against.role: Industry whose revenue depends on Part D prices
against.what_they_did: Opposed government negotiation of Medicare drug prices and lobbied to keep the current noninterference law in place; the industry's sustained lobbying is widely credited with keeping such proposals from advancing in this era.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so there is no roll call to divide; the sponsorship pattern points one way, with all eight cosponsors Democrats or Independents and no Republicans, and the bill dying in a committee chaired by a Democrat without action.

industries.note: The bill would have forced manufacturers to negotiate prices and discounts on Medicare-covered drugs, the largest group purchase of prescriptions in the country. Its interest runs against the public's here: keeping negotiation off the books preserves the current prices that seniors' premiums and federal subsidies pay for.

industries.industry: Private Medicare Part D plan sponsors and pharmacy benefit managers
industries.note: Government-set negotiated prices would constrain the plans' and intermediaries' role as price-setters, but the bill preserved their freedom to negotiate discounts below the government's price. Enrollees would benefit if the savings flowed through to lower premiums and cost-sharing.
